overview: Tsimshian communities belong to the Skeena River and northern British Columbia coast, with a later community at Metlakatla, Alaska. Related Gitxsan and Nisg̱a’a peoples remain distinct neighbors. This map outlines part of a diverse homeland; its 1492 to 1500 interval is coverage, not a people’s lifetime.

periods.title: Villages around the waterways
periods.summary: Ancient settlements and later winter villages preserve a long record of occupation around Metlakatla Pass.

periods.title: Trade and powerful alliances
periods.summary: Nine Tribes leaders shaped maritime and inland exchange, including the trade around Fort Simpson.

periods.title: Missions, migration and new institutions
periods.summary: Metlakatla became a mission settlement in 1862; part of its community moved to Alaska in 1887.

periods.title: Distinct communities continue
periods.summary: Community government, fishing and other work sustain Metlakatla in Alaska alongside the continuing First Nations in British Columbia.

items.text: On Pike Island, three former village sites and two petroglyph sites lie along the protected waters of Metlakatla Pass. Trails connect settlement remains; carved images survive on shoreline boulders. The largest village area, used both before and after European contact, measures about 211 by 70 metres.

Around the wider pass, archaeological remains include house depressions, canoe landing places and shell middens. Parks Canada identifies a particularly dense sequence of winter villages from about 500 to 1770. These traces connect homes, boats and meals across a worked coastal landscape.

Kitselas Canyon guarded a route between the coast and the interior. Its surviving evidence includes five village sites, carved poles, caches and house depressions. In the nineteenth century, the fortified village of Gitlaxdzok and another permanent village occupied positions from which residents could influence trade through the Skeena corridor.

The Nine Tribes of Lax Kw’alaams built power through alliances, strategic marriages and military action. Their trade connections followed routes carrying valuable eulachon oil into the interior. Community history emphasizes these relationships and decisions, rather than explaining political power simply as a result of plentiful fish.

In 1834, the Hudson’s Bay Company built Fort Simpson at Lax Kw’alaams on a site controlled by the Gispaxlo’ots leader Legex. He required payments for trading there. Tsimshian people also supplied wood and labor; their seasonal activities shaped how the fort could operate.

Tsimshian clan membership comes through the mother. The four clans are associated with Killer Whale, Wolf, Eagle and Raven. Crests can identify a clan or an extended family and carry histories and inherited rights; they are much more than decorative animal pictures.

At Metlakatla potlatches, guests witness proceedings such as naming and succession. Hosts feed them and provide gifts in thanks. Dance, masks and family histories help make those rights publicly known, so a feast also performs serious political and legal work.

Gitga’at families travel to Kiel camp on Princess Royal Island for spring harvesting. Their Nation’s 2024 account describes collecting red laver seaweed in May and preserving food for later months. Harvesting joins practical work with time together and opportunities for younger relatives to learn.

The same account describes slicing halibut thin for drying after returning to Hartley Bay, then smoking heads and backbones for soup. It also recalls exchanging harvested seaweed at Kitamaat for eulachon grease. A fishing trip could supply several kinds of meal and goods for trade.

A 2023 Gitga’at food guide describes dayks, a dessert of berries with whipped grease, snow or water and sugar. The recipe illustrates the community’s living food traditions, including later ingredients. Snow can enter the dessert bowl, but this modern description is not evidence for sugar in a precontact kitchen.

William Duncan’s mission at Metlakatla, British Columbia, began in 1862. In 1887, he and part of the Tsimshian community moved to Alaska; others remained in British Columbia. Metlakatla Pass and Pike Island retain their connection to the Canadian Metlakatla First Nation, so the move did not empty an entire homeland.

The Alaska community’s 1944 constitution records the establishment of its Annette Islands reserve in 1891. It provided for a twelve-member council, elected officials and community management of land. These institutions belong to a particular Tsimshian community, not to a government ruling all Tsimshian peoples.

Public health had its own place in that constitution. A three-member committee was to help preserve birth and death records, cooperate with health officials, maintain sanitary conditions and enforce quarantine rules. Community government included the everyday work of keeping households and public spaces healthy.

A modern Sm’algya̱x language exhibit prints “‘Niit, nda wila waan”, translated “Hello, how are you doing?” The museum credits the Ts’msyen language authority, Sarah Booth and the Haayk Foundation for its language material. This is an attested contemporary spelling, not a claimed fifteenth-century inscription.

At Gitxaała’s Lach Klan School, education from early childhood through Grade 12 includes language, culture and learning on the land alongside provincial requirements. Its published programs also include breakfast, snacks and fruit and vegetables. Teaching and feeding children are part of the same daily community work.

Canadian Metlakatla’s heritage staff combine elder interviews, community mapping and archival research, storing knowledge in digital maps for land and marine decisions. They also monitor archaeological resources such as canoe runs, fish traps and culturally modified trees. New tools help communities care for inherited places.

ending.text: The map’s 1500 cutoff is not an ending. Colonial missions, settlement and restrictions changed Tsimshian lives, while distinct First Nations in British Columbia and the Metlakatla Indian Community in Alaska continued. Their governments, cultural teaching and stewardship remain active; no single successor state replaces them.
